sentences.text: You're correct - the MVP I outlined is just server-based STT displayed in the PWA.
And you've hit on a critical limitation: PWAs have significant restrictions on background functionality, especially for continuous audio recording.

## PWA Background Limitations
Continuous audio recording (browsers suspend MediaStream when backgrounded)
WebRTC connections (typically disconnected when tab loses focus)
WebSocket connections (throttled or closed after ~30 seconds)
JavaScript execution (heavily throttled or paused)
Service Workers can run briefly for specific events
Push notifications can wake the app
Background sync for queued data upload
Limited background fetch (periodic, not continuous)



Your extended cognition concept requires always-on listening, which PWAs simply cannot deliver.
When the user switches apps or locks their phone, audio capture stops.

## Alternative Approaches
PWA for active conversations (tab in foreground)
Native companion app for background recording
Sync between them via shared backend
PWA stays dormant
User says "Hey Claude" to activate
Similar to Alexa/Siri model
Keep tablet/phone with PWA always open
Screen stays on, app in foreground
Works for desk/home scenarios

Start with Foreground-Only PWA (Week 1-4)
Proves the pipeline works
Tests latency and performance
No platform-specific complexity
Add Electron Wrapper (Week 5-8)
Enables true background recording on desktop
Minimal code changes from PWA
Good for demos and personal use
Consider Mobile Native (Post-demo)

DURING match: Rhythmic breathing that matches intensity (functional)

Offscreen Document (always running):
Continuous audio recording
Transcription processing
Media button listening
Screen wake attempts
Service Worker (wakes on demand):
Module execution when needed
State management when active
Goes back to sleep when done
Wake Triggers:
Voice command detected ("wake up screen")
Important notification needed
User interaction required







Full screen wake from deep sleep: Not possible with Chrome Extension APIs

Practical alternatives that work:
Notification wake - Shows notification that wakes screen
Audio feedback - Play sound through headphones ("Meeting in 5 minutes")
LED indicator - If device has notification LED
Minimal always-on display - Small overlay that prevents full sleep



Structure your modules with these assumptions:
Offscreen document = Always-on brain stem (audio, basic reflexes)
Service worker modules = Higher brain functions (wake as needed)
Wake strategies = Notifications + audio feedback
Graceful degradation = If screen won't wake, at least notify through audio

This way your Voice Brain can maintain awareness even during sleep states, and attempt to get user attention when needed without relying on impossible screen wake APIs.

Let me address your questions directly and honestly.
VLM as narrator: The VLM (Vision-Language Model) handles both vision AND language, so it's doing scene understanding plus intent parsing in one model.
Figure's Helix uses a 7B VLM that looks at cameras and understands "pick up the red cup" simultaneously.
The trajectory planner below it is a smaller specialized model that just does vision-to-action, no language reasoning.
So yes, two separate concerns: semantic understanding (VLM) and motor planning (visuomotor policy).
80M parameter at 200 Hz: The 80M model outputs joint position targets, not raw motor commands.
The motors receive those targets and their internal controllers (or your hybrid neural-PID) execute them.
200 Hz means the policy updates its target 200 times per second, giving very smooth motion.
The motors themselves can respond much faster (1-10 kHz internal loops).
Helix cost: Figure AI hasn't published pricing, it's not available for purchase.
They're deploying it in BMW factories under commercial contracts.

Subgoal and action durations - let me be precise here because you asked me to check you:

Looking at the actual research:
π0.5 predicts subtasks that span 2-10 seconds typically
The VLA outputs action chunks of 50-100 timesteps at 10-50 Hz, roughly 1-2 seconds of motion per inference
Motor group policies in Helix output at 200 Hz continuously, not in chunks

So the timing is: Narrator fires on task change or completion (variable, could be 5 seconds to 5 minutes).
VLA/trajectory runs every 0.5-2 seconds, outputting the next 1-2 seconds of motion.
Motor execution is continuous at 100-200 Hz.
Why not all running at the same timeframe: Different computational costs.
The narrator (8B params) takes 100-500ms to run.
The VLA (100-500M params) takes 30-100ms.
The motor group (5-50M) takes 5-10ms.
The joint controller (100K-1M + PID) takes 0.1-1ms.
If you tried to run the narrator at 200 Hz, you'd need impossible compute.
The hierarchy exists because different decisions need different amounts of thinking time.
Proprioception: Yes, it's the robot's sense of its own body position.
Joint angles, velocities, motor currents.
Not touch exactly, that's tactile sensing, but internal body awareness.
What makes robots slower on the production line: Not the control frequency.

It's:
Vision processing latency (30-100ms to understand a scene)
Conservatism in the policy (trained to be safe, not fast)
Settling time (waiting for vibrations to damp before precision moves)
Human-imposed speed limits for safety certification

Industrial robots CAN move extremely fast.
UR5 max speed is 1 m/s, some industrial arms hit 5+ m/s.
The limitation is usually the task, not the hardware.
Hidden units: Neurons in a layer that isn't input or output.
A 2-layer MLP with 32 hidden units means: input layer → 32 neurons → 32 neurons → output layer.
Each hidden unit computes a weighted sum of inputs, applies a nonlinearity, passes to the next layer.
Zero-shot transfer: The MeMo paper trained a controller on a 6-legged robot.
Then they added 2 more legs to the simulation (8 legs total).
Without any additional training, the same per-joint policies worked because each joint's controller only sees local information.
The network didn't need to "learn" 8 legs because each leg's controller is independent.
That's what modular architecture enables.
Morphology: Body shape/structure.
A spider has different morphology than a humanoid.
Morphology transfer means a controller trained on one body shape working on a different body shape.
Is the narrator what creates subgoals: Yes, or an intermediate planner layer.
The narrator outputs structured intent like "pick up red block, place in bin" which might decompose into subgoals: (1) move to block, (2) grasp, (3) lift, (4) move to bin, (5) release.
Some systems do this decomposition explicitly (SayCan, π0.5), others let the VLA figure it out implicitly.
Manufacturing box cameras: Yes, one overhead workspace camera plus wrist cameras per arm works.
The workspace camera feeds into the shared VLA for scene understanding.
Wrist cameras feed into arm-specific policies for close manipulation.
This is exactly how ALOHA and similar systems work.
Proprioception as VLA input: Correct.
The VLA takes camera images AND current joint states AND the narrative/intent.
It needs to know where the arm currently is to plan where it should go.
Why rerun motor group policy: You're right to question this.

Two approaches in practice:
Run once per trajectory chunk (every 1-2s), output all 100-200 timesteps, execute open-loop
Run continuously at 30-100 Hz, output next 10-50 timesteps, always replanning

Approach 2 is more robust because it corrects for disturbances.
You're constantly updating your plan based on what actually happened.
The "future projection" you mention is implicit, the policy learns to output trajectories that account for expected dynamics.
Joint controller anomaly filtering: Separate from output.
You monitor motor current and position error.
If current spikes unexpectedly (hit something) or position error grows (motor stalling), that's an anomaly signal that propagates up.
The joint controller doesn't filter its own output, it reports problems upward.
Is this actually happening: Yes.
Figure AI is deploying Helix at BMW.
Physical Intelligence demonstrated π0 doing laundry folding.
These are real systems in real environments.
The research I'm citing is from 2024-2025, published and peer-reviewed.
This isn't hype, it's the current state of deployed robotics.
DAgger-style learning: Dataset Aggregation.
The key insight: if you only train on expert demonstrations, the robot never learns to recover from mistakes because the expert never made mistakes.

DAgger works like this:
Expert demonstrates task, collect data
Train policy on expert data
Robot executes policy while expert watches
When robot deviates, expert corrects (provides the "right" action from that wrong state)
Add correction data to training set
Retrain, repeat

The correction data teaches recovery.
Your "operation buzzer" idea is exactly this, except instead of providing the correct action, you're providing a negative signal.
That works too, it's called learning from human feedback.
The 10-minute training intuition is optimistic but not crazy for simple tasks.
Research shows 20-50 demonstrations for basic pick-place with DAgger-style correction.
Operation game by year end: Honestly?
Possible but aggressive.

Operation requires:
~1mm precision (tweezers in narrow slots)
Force sensitivity (don't touch the edges)
Visual recognition of which piece to grab

With good hardware (XM540-class servos, RealSense depth), proper training pipeline, maybe 100-200 demonstrations with haptic feedback, you could get 70-80% success rate in 6 months of focused work.
95%+ is harder.
Spider climbing stairs in 10 seconds: Easier than Operation, ironically.
Locomotion is more forgiving than manipulation.
Hexapod platforms exist (PhantomX ~$2000).
Stair climbing is a solved problem for 6+ legged robots.
10 seconds for a standard staircase is achievable with existing open-source controllers.
The MeMo-style modular approach would let you train in simulation and transfer to real hardware.

What you should build first:
Motion capture rig ($100-150): SlimeVR IMUs on wrist, elbow, shoulder, plus finger tracking for gripper
Single arm with teleoperation: SO-101 class ($300-500) with leader-follower or direct IMU mapping  
Training pipeline: LeRobot or custom, doesn't matter, just get demonstration → policy working
Simple task: Pick and place blocks, not Operation.
Get the full loop working first.
The spider is actually a good parallel project because it's different enough that you're learning two complementary things: manipulation (arm) and locomotion (spider).
And the modular architecture research applies to both.

The Setup

A 6-DOF desktop arm is basically your entry point to real robotic manipulation.
Six degrees of freedom means three axes of position (X, Y, Z) plus three axes of rotation, so it can reach most points in its workspace from most angles.
The 3D-printable stuff (like the ones based on designs from folks building open-source arms) cuts cost from tens of thousands down to maybe $500-2000 in components.
This is genuinely achievable now because brushless motors got cheap, 3D printing tolerances got tight enough, and you can run everything on a Jetson or even a good laptop.
The ML question is actually trickier than it sounds.
You don't want an LLM unless you're doing high-level task planning—like telling it "pick up the red block and put it in the box.
" For the actual arm control, you're looking at behavior cloning or reinforcement learning, where the arm learns from demonstrations or trial-and-error.
Computer vision (pose estimation, object detection) feeds the arm what it's looking at.
The LLM layer sits on top if you need language understanding, but the arm's decision-making is typically smaller models trained on movement patterns.
Open source is mature here.
Projects like xArm, OpenManipulator, and various custom designs from researchers are all out there.
You can grab trained models for basic tasks from robotics platforms, but honestly, the real work is in training your arm for *your specific setup*—your workspace, your objects, your lighting.
The ecosystem is collaborative but still requires patience.

What They Actually Do

These arms are weirdly good at precision repetitive tasks once trained.
Pick and place, sorting objects by visual features, assembly-like work—they nail this.

The surprise is how much planning goes into motion: the arm doesn't just move to a point, it has to compute collision-free paths, account for its own bulk, and deal with the fact that grabbing an object changes its dynamics.
People are shocked when they see one do fine-motor control like threading a needle or stacking blocks neatly.
What kills people's expectations: they're terrible at improvisation.
Put a slightly different object in front of one trained on red blocks, and it might freeze or grab it wrong.
They struggle with deformable stuff (cloth, rope, anything soft).
Real-world grime, lighting changes, and slight variations in object placement wreck trained models faster than you'd think.
They also can't really understand context the way humans do—if you ask one to "organize the desk," it doesn't know what organized means.
The other surprise: speed is slow.
A trained arm might take 10-30 seconds per pick-and-place task.
They look glacial compared to human hands.
And they fail silently sometimes—they'll go through motions but miss the object because the depth estimation was off by 2 centimeters.
Recovery isn't automatic.
You're also locked into whatever task you trained it for; generalization is the hard frontier nobody's cracked yet.
